_comment: SHARED FIXTURE - one answer key for the session subsystem, all four frameworks.
ADR-0024: swapping file for redis, valkey, mongodb, memcached or database
changes ONE env var and NOTHING ELSE. Identical application code, identical
These are INVARIANTS, not a bug list. Six defects were measured here on
2026-08-01 and each is an instance of one of the rules below being broken.
Sessions carry a second weight the other subsystems do not: a session defect
is usually a SECURITY defect. A session that does not expire when told, or one
that silently becomes empty, is an auth outcome rather than a storage one.
HOW THIS IS CHECKED: see scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py. An invariant with
an empty 'cases' list is OWED - declared, not yet proven. A case that was named
and has since disappeared FAILS the build.

invariants.rule: TINA4_SESSION_TTL is honoured by EVERY backend. A session expires when the configured TTL says so, on file, redis, valkey, mongodb, memcached and database alike.
invariants.why: MEASURED: in Ruby the TTL is honoured by the memcached backend ONLY - every other backend hard-codes 86400. An operator setting a 15-minute session gets 24 hours on five of six backends, and nothing reports it. This is a security outcome expressed as a storage default.
cases: session ttl env var expires the record on every backend
session ttl env var keeps a long lived record on every backend
session ttl env var reaches the stored deadline out of band
session ttl option on the session reaches the stored record
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-04 on the lab host (Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64) against a LIVE Redis 7, Valkey 8, memcached 1.6.45, MongoDB 7, PostgreSQL 16 and real SQLite files, TINA4_REQUIRE_SERVICES=1, real wall-clock expiry with no clock mocking anywhere. RE-MEASURED at v3 HEAD before any fix and the defect was still there at the line: Ruby read TINA4_SESSION_TTL in exactly ONE handler (memcached), while file, redis, mongodb and database each hard-coded `@ttl = options[:ttl] || 86400` and valkey read a Ruby-only TINA4_SESSION_VALKEY_TTL; the first run of the new spec went red with 'TINA4_SESSION_TTL=2 was ignored by: file, database, redis, valkey, mongodb' and 'file stored now+86400s, database stored now+86400s, redis stored now+86400s, valkey stored now+86400s'. FOUND AS WELL, and NOT in the original finding: Ruby's Session#save called safe_write(@id, @data) with NO ttl, so an explicit Session.new(ttl:) never reached the store at all - the cookie carried Max-Age and the record did not. Ruby's mongodb handler ALSO had no read-time expiry check, delegating entirely to a TTL index; mongod's TTL monitor sweeps once per 60 SECONDS, so a 2-second session stayed readable for up to a minute past expiry, and it stored updated_at where Python, PHP and Node all store an absolute expires_at. AND Python was broken too, narrowly: FileSessionHandler and DatabaseSessionHandler had no ttl at all, so a bare write(id, data) stored _expires = 0 meaning NEVER EXPIRES while the identical call on memcached expired in an hour - fixed in Python rather than mirrored, per the Python-is-master-unless-Python-is-broken rule. PHP already satisfied the invariant and is a pure lock-in. Node satisfies it end-to-end through Session, which is the only place it reads TINA4_SESSION_TTL for five of six backends; its HANDLER-boundary half is OWED and tracked by ADR-0027, because Node deliberately reads a zero ttl as 'never expires' and pins that with session_mongo_zero_ttl_never_expires - flipping a deliberate, test-locked decision needed an ADR, not a silent change. MUTATION-PROVED in every framework, each mutation asserted to APPLY before running: reverting Ruby's file default kills 2 cases naming 'file' and redis's kills 2 naming redis; removing Ruby's mongo read-time guard kills 1 naming mongodb; reverting Ruby's or Python's save-forwarding kills EXACTLY the Session-level case and nothing else; dropping Python's file or database default kills 2 naming that backend. Recorded because it nearly fooled me: the first Ruby mutation attempt used sed with a `|` delimiter against code containing `||`, silently failed to apply, and reported a meaningless 4-examples-0-failures green - a mutation that does not apply is not a mutation. Python 4772 passed / 27 skipped; Ruby 4908 examples / 0 failures / 8 pending at two different seeds, baseline 4904; PHP 4839 tests / 15295 assertions / 0 failures / 37 skipped; Node 7069 passed / 0 failed across 237 files.

invariants.rule: A TTL is expressed in the same units by the caller regardless of provider, and each backend converts to whatever its wire protocol needs.
invariants.why: MEASURED: memcached treats any TTL above 2592000 seconds (30 days) as an ABSOLUTE UNIX timestamp. A raw TTL above that threshold is read as a moment in 1970, so the session expires instantly. The caller wrote a number of seconds; the provider read a date. Providers differ - the contract must not.

invariants.rule: A backend that becomes unreachable mid-request is LOGGED and then degraded: the read yields an empty session, save() returns false, and the request still serves. It is never silent. TINA4_SESSION_STRICT re-raises instead.
invariants.why: MEASURED: in Python a session-backend failure on the real HTTP path is SILENT - request.session becomes None with nothing logged. An operator sees users mysteriously logged out and has no signal at all. A genuinely EMPTY session is not an error and must never be logged as one - that distinction is the whole point.

invariants.rule: A session handler performs no network I/O in its constructor. Connection happens on first use, inside the log-loud-and-degrade policy.
invariants.why: MEASURED: the database backend does network I/O in the HANDLER CONSTRUCTOR, which sits OUTSIDE the failure policy. So the one place the policy cannot protect is the first thing that runs, and an unreachable backend takes the app down at construction rather than degrading per-request as designed.

invariants.rule: A backend that advertises support for an engine works on that engine. The database session backend works on every engine the Database layer supports, not a subset.
invariants.why: MEASURED: Node's database session backend is SQLite-only and THROWS at Session construction on any other engine. Develop on sqlite, deploy on postgres, and the app does not start - the founding scenario of ADR-0024, in the subsystem that decides whether anyone is logged in.

invariants.rule: Where three frameworks ship a zero-dependency transport for a backend, the fourth does too. A backend must not hard-require a third-party client in one framework and not the others.
invariants.why: MEASURED: Ruby's mongodb session backend hard-requires the `mongo` gem while the other three ship a zero-dependency wire-protocol fallback. The same .env therefore works in three frameworks and raises in the fourth - and it breaks the zero-dependency promise asymmetrically, which is worse than breaking it consistently.
